speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: ISP is about not making classes implement things they don't need, which sounds obvious until you see a Robot implementing eat() and sleep().

beats.content: Interface Segregation Principle says no client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use. Instead of one fat interface with many methods, create small focused interfaces. Each class picks only the ones it needs.

The Robot example makes it concrete. A fat Worker interface has work(), eat(), and sleep(). Robot has to implement all three but has no concept of eating or sleeping. It ends up throwing UnsupportedOperationException in those methods. That's the ISP violation.

candidates miss: the key idea isn't just that interfaces should be small. It's that clients shouldn't carry methods they don't use. Split into Workable, Eatable, Sleepable. Robot implements Workable only. Human implements all three. Each class gets exactly what it needs.

speakable_v2.cap: ISP: small focused interfaces so classes never implement methods they don't use and never need to throw UnsupportedOperationException.
followup_handoff: How does ISP relate to the Single Responsibility Principle?

question: What is the Interface Segregation Principle?
title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) — small focused interfaces
direct_answer: **ISP** says **no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use**. Instead of one large interface with many methods, create **smaller, focused interfaces**. A class should only implement the interface(s) relevant to what it actually does.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand ISP as being about client burden, not interface size alone
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying ISP just means interfaces should be small — the key is that clients should not be forced to implement methods they do not use
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example with a fat interface and a class forced to throw UnsupportedOperationException

sections.title: ISP violation vs ISP correct
How to say this in an interview
sections.content: Interface Segregation Principle says: do not force a class to implement methods it does not need. If I have one big Worker interface with work, eat, and sleep, a Robot class that implements Worker has to implement eat and sleep even though robots do not do those things. The fix is to split the fat interface into smaller ones — Workable, Eatable, Sleepable — and have Robot only implement Workable. Each class picks only the interfaces it actually needs.

question: What is a fat interface and why is it a problem?
title: Fat interfaces — what they are and why they violate ISP
direct_answer: A **fat interface** (or bloated interface) is one that has **too many methods** covering multiple responsibilities. Implementing classes are forced to provide implementations for methods they do not need, leading to empty methods or UnsupportedOperationException. It also makes the interface harder to understand and change.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being able to name the pattern — interviewers like candidates who know the vocabulary
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect fat interfaces to the God Object antipattern — both pack too much into one thing

sections.title: Problems with fat interfaces
sections.content: Fat interfaces have three main problems: 1) Implementing classes are burdened with methods they do not need. 2) Changing one method in the fat interface forces all implementers to recompile/re-implement even if they do not use that method. 3) The interface becomes hard to understand — when everything is in one place, nothing is clear. The fix is always to split by concern.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: A fat interface is one that has grown to include methods from multiple different concerns. The problem is that every class implementing it gets forced to provide all those methods, even the irrelevant ones. You end up with empty stub methods or UnsupportedOperationException in many places. It also makes the codebase brittle — a change to any method in the fat interface forces recompilation of everything implementing it. Small, focused interfaces are easier to implement, test, and change.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: Every method you add to a fat interface is a forced change for every class that implements it, even the ones that don't care.

beats.content: With segregated interfaces, a change to one interface only affects the classes that actually implement it. Add a method to Eatable and only Human and Animal need to update. Robot and Machine are completely untouched.

With a fat Worker interface used by 30 classes, adding one method forces all 30 classes to change. In a large codebase that means 30 files to update, 30 tests to run, and 30 places where a developer might introduce a bug.

sharp edge: in a compiled language like Java, this also affects compilation. When an interface changes, every class implementing it has to recompile. Smaller interfaces mean smaller compilation scope and faster builds in large projects.

speakable_v2.cap: ISP limits the blast radius of interface changes: small interfaces mean fewer classes are affected when you add or modify a method.

question: How does ISP improve the flexibility of a codebase?
title: ISP and codebase flexibility — smaller interfaces, fewer forced changes
direct_answer: Small interfaces mean **fewer classes are affected** when you add or change methods. If you add a method to a small, focused interface, only the few classes that implement it need to change. With a fat interface, adding one method forces every single implementing class to change — even those that have no business with that method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connecting ISP to the practical benefit of fewer forced changes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving only a theoretical answer without the change-impact argument
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Quantify the impact: one fat interface used by 20 classes means 20 classes must be updated for every method added

sections.title: Change impact with ISP
sections.content: With segregated interfaces, each implementing class only depends on the methods it actually uses. Adding a new method to the Eatable interface affects only Human and Animal — not Robot or Machine. If you had a fat Worker interface used by 20 classes, adding eat() would require all 20 classes to add an implementation. ISP limits the blast radius of interface changes.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: ISP makes a codebase more flexible by reducing the blast radius of changes. If I have one big interface used by 30 classes and I need to add a method, all 30 classes must update. With segregated interfaces, I add the method to a small interface used by only 3 classes — only 3 things change. This is especially important in large codebases where you want to limit how far a change ripples.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: Spring Data JPA was actually designed with ISP in mind. Most developers just don't notice.

beats.content: Spring Data JPA has a deliberate interface hierarchy: CrudRepository for basic save and find, PagingAndSortingRepository adds pagination, and JpaRepository adds the full set including JPQL and batch operations. That's ISP in practice.

The common mistake is always extending JpaRepository for every repository, even when you only need findById and save. You pull in 30-plus methods your service never uses. For read-heavy services, a custom narrow interface with just the two methods you need is cleaner and safer.

non-obvious: defining a ReadOnlyUserRepository interface with only findById and findByEmail is an ISP move that also adds safety. A service depending on it literally cannot call save() or delete() by mistake. The interface boundary enforces behavior.

speakable_v2.cap: In Spring, extend only the repository interface you need. Use narrow interfaces for read-only services to enforce boundaries at the type level.
followup_handoff: What is the difference between CrudRepository and JpaRepository?
How do you define a read-only repository in Spring?

question: How does ISP apply to Spring Boot application design?
title: ISP in Spring Boot — Repository interfaces and service interfaces
direct_answer: In Spring Boot, ISP is visible in the JPA repository hierarchy: **JpaRepository** extends **PagingAndSortingRepository** which extends **CrudRepository**. If a class only needs basic CRUD, it should implement CrudRepository — not JpaRepository with 30 methods it never uses. Same for service interfaces — define narrow interfaces per use case.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to connect SOLID principles to the Spring framework you will use day to day
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using JpaRepository even when simple CRUD is all that is needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention read-only interfaces as an ISP application — a service that only reads should get a ReadOnlyUserRepository

sections.content: Spring Data JPA is actually designed with ISP in mind — there is CrudRepository for basic operations, PagingAndSortingRepository for pagination, and JpaRepository for the full set. A common ISP anti-pattern is to always use JpaRepository even when you only need to save and find. For read-heavy services, I prefer to define a narrow interface with just findById and findByEmail, so the service only knows about what it actually needs.

speakable_v2.hook: SRP and ISP look similar until you realize one talks about classes and the other about interfaces.

rows: class does too many things, has multiple reasons to change
clients forced to implement methods they don't use

beats.content: SRP is about cohesion in a class: one class, one responsibility, one reason to change. ISP is about cohesion in an interface: one interface, one concern, no unused methods forced on clients.

gotcha: they often appear together. A fat interface usually reflects a class that does too much. When you refactor, you might split the class first (SRP) and then split the interface to match (ISP). Knowing that they're related but distinct shows depth of understanding.

speakable_v2.cap: SRP: one class, one reason to change. ISP: one interface, no methods your client doesn't need. Different tools, often applied together.

question: How is ISP different from SRP?
title: ISP vs SRP — interface segregation vs single responsibility
direct_answer: **SRP applies to classes** — a class should have one reason to change. **ISP applies to interfaces** — clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. A fat interface violates ISP. A class that does too many things violates SRP. They are related: splitting a fat interface often means each resulting interface aligns with one responsibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish the two principles and articulate their scope
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing them as the same principle — they apply to different things
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how violating ISP (fat interface) and violating SRP (class does too much) often appear together

sections.title: SRP vs ISP comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | SRP | ISP |
|--------|-----|-----|
| Applies to | Classes | Interfaces |
| Concern | Too many reasons to change | Clients forced to depend on unused methods |
| Violation sign | Class does too many things | Fat interface with unrelated methods |
| Fix | Split the class | Split the interface |
| Goal | Cohesive class | Cohesive interface |

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: SRP is about classes — a class should have one reason to change and one responsibility. ISP is about interfaces — a client should not be forced to depend on methods it does not use. They are related: a fat interface often reflects a class that does too much. But the fix is different — SRP says split the class, ISP says split the interface. You often need to apply both together when refactoring.
